newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH M2 DECLINE NOT YET SLOWING INFLATION - C.BANK.
newsitem.headline: CZECH M2 DECLINE NOT YET SLOWING INFLATION - C.BANK.

text.p: Czech National Bank Governor Josef Tosovsky said that he was pleased with the rapid deceleration in money supply growth, but said it has yet to clearly translate into lower consumer inflation.

In a taped interview with Reuters Financial Television to be brodcast later, Tosovsky said that he expected the key measure of money supply, M2, to be at the "lower edge" of the central bank's 13 to 17 percent target range for growth by the end of the year.

"We are now seeing the environment for the delcine in inflation, but I must confess... we don't have, I would say clear empirical evidence and a correlation between money supply decline and inflation," Tosovsky said.
The M2 growth rate has slowed dramatically to an overall 11.8 percent, year-on-year, at the end of September, according to figures released on Thursday from than 20 percent growth mid-year.
But Tosovsky said the closure of some smaller banks, and the dampening effect of strong import levels on prices amid an accelerating trade deficit actually had helped the overall inflation outlook.
"We changed our monetary policy (in June) by raising minimum reserve requirements and by raising interest rates, and the results are visible," Tosovsky said.
"The (rate of growth in the) money supply is going down very quickly, and we will probably be at the end of this year at the lower edge of the corridor or band for money supply."

Consumer prices slowed to an 8.7 percent year-on-year rate in September from 8.9 percent in August and well over nine percent earlier in the year, but still one of the lowest rates in post-Communist Europe.
But the governor said that the Czech economy still had some imbalances which blocked the correlation between slower growth in the money supply and lower inflation common in industrialised economies.
Tosovsky declined to forecast any inflation figure for 1997, but said that it was the central bank's goal to get the rate down "closer to EU levels".

The CNB had set a target for lowering annual inflation by the end of 1996 to eight percent, but strong consumer demand in the first half, and government deregulations combined to keep prices stubbornly high.
